_how: The words and every note of the feedback page. Build: node hub/feedback.mjs --out <folder>.
A new note: add it to "notes" (any order, the build sorts newest first). Copy the text as typed, typos and all.
kind: bug, idea or other. state: open, handled, or check (the relay deploy's own notes, never counted).
A note that is fixed and live: state "handled" and "fixed" the version that fixed it, like 1.0.410. The page crosses it out.
tag: one short line under the note, or "". related: the numbers of notes about the same thing.
shortened: true when the reader cut the note off. The page ends it with an ellipsis.
Every count on the page is worked out from this list. Type none. Then set "updated".
title: Portage

intro: Every note play testers have sent from the game’s Feedback menu, newest first. A note that is crossed out is fixed and live.

notes.text: You need a Workload Management framework where you can log/track your bugs and enhancements.  You can include timeline, categorize them, and mark them by severity as well.

THE JOB
Rework my friend Luc's browser canoe game, Portage (git@github.com:LucSigouin/portage.git), so the lake is Lake Opeongo in Algonquin Park, Ontario, instead of the current flooded valley. Research the real lake first, then build the map and the new systems below.

Map and world:
- Base the shoreline, the arms and where the islands sit on the real Opeongo outline. Sproule Bay is the start in the south. The South Arm runs north from it to the Narrows, with the island cluster near Bates Island. The East Arm wraps around Opeongo Island and runs east to Annie Bay and the dam. The North Arm is the big northwest basin. Hailstorm Creek's long bay runs off to the west. Jones Bay and Sludge Bay are in their real spots.
- Scale it about 1:5 so the real lake (about 15 x 15 km) fits the game's world (about 3 x 3 km).
- Use Algonquin's real trees and plants. Trees: white and red pine, hemlock, sugar maple, yellow and white birch, white cedar along the shore, black spruce and tamarack in the bogs. Smaller plants: blueberry, bunchberry, sweet gale, leatherleaf, pickerelweed, water lilies, and lichen on the granite.
- At the narrow start, where the channel leaves Sproule Bay, put 20-foot (about 6 m) cliffs on both sides.
- I can land on the mainland shore too, not just on islands.
- Add caves along the shore that I can canoe into.
- Add fire towers I can climb to look around.

Landing:
- Each island has exactly one landing spot. On the mainland, the only landing spots are ones that matter for progression or for collecting materials.
- Every other bit of shore is blocked by things you can see: thick trees, fallen logs, small cliffs or steep rock. No invisible walls (BRIEF.md pillar 4).
- When I land, the canoe skids about halfway up onto the land, with a short scraping sound.
- When I leave, my guy plays a short animation of pushing the canoe off, then climbs in.
- Each landing has a narrow trail to its landmark or material area. The forest is dense, and the trails are what op
